items.note: Newly discovered serpentine (nagabandha) letter-diagram inscription on a sandstone slab in the Udayesvara parapet wall, called varnanagakrpanika, a 'serpentine scimitar of letters'.

Identical composition at Ujjain tied to Udayaditya (c. 1070-93) and Naravarman (1094-1134); similar pieces at Dhar and Un place Udaypur's in the late 11th century; read as devices of dynastic power at royal Shiva temples.
Temple (Nilakantheshvara/Udayeshvara) described as built around 1080 in the bhumija style associated with the Paramara dynasty (Deva 1975).

Continuous sequence of inscriptions in Sanskrit, Persian and Hindi over eight centuries, from consecration in samvat 1137 to restoration in samvat 1985; listed in Gwalior State and ASI epigraphy reports, only partly published.
Inscribed slab built into the outer parapet wall, evidently reset during restoration campaigns under Gwalior State.
Nagabandha/sarpabandha composition; palaeography compared to late-11th-century local records with well-formed inch-high rectilinear characters; orthographic peculiarities.
Describes the diagram: vowels as head, consonants as body, 21 noun and 18 verb terminations at the tail, following the classical alphabet arrangement.
Short metrical verse naming the varnanagakrpanika with pala/palayatu; sense 'may the protector cause this serpentine sword of letters to protect'.
Designation read as a weapon for protection, serpentine and letterist: hood as vowels, body as consonants, tail as terminations.

Ujjain twin names the diagram as marked with Udayaditya's name; lines 24-26 call it a unique magical sword of Shiva's worshippers, kings Udayaditya and Naravarman, for preservation of language and social order.
Argues it served the Paramara kings rather than being a school tool; copies at Ujjain and Udaypur, a town whose temple and tank were founded and named after Udayaditya in 1080.

claim.value: temple and tank founded and named after Udayaditya in 1080
